title: Chemistry Foundations: Introduction to Matter Complete Instructional Unit
cover_credit: Particle classification visual: John Trombley, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
cover_features: 12 student lesson, practice, and review pages
Unit Tests A and B with 20 multiple-choice items each
Teacher guide, full answers, rationales, and repair moves
cover_claim: Move from what students can see to particle-level claims they can defend.
unit_purpose: Students build a coherent model of matter by connecting macroscopic observations with particle representations, composition, physical and chemical properties, change evidence, and property-based separation methods.

pacing.plan: Lesson 1: Matter at Two Scales. Use the particle visual to separate observable evidence from model assumptions.
Lesson 2: Classify Matter by Composition. Require evidence for every label.
Lesson 3: Properties Describe Matter. Contrast property with change and intensive with extensive.
Lesson 4: Physical or Chemical Change. Treat common clues as evidence, not automatic proof.
Lesson 5: Separate Mixtures by Properties. Link each method to the property difference it exploits.
Cumulative mixed review, feedback, and targeted reteaching.
Unit Test A. Reserve Form B for a retake, alternate class, or test security.

before_teaching: Preview the particle-model conventions and the documented instructional visuals. Decide whether students will work individually or discuss the engage prompts in pairs. Emphasize that a model is useful evidence but is not a literal, to-scale photograph.
look_fors: Students distinguish uniform from pure, property from change, physical clue from chemical proof, and a separation method from the property difference that makes it work.
support: Keep the composition decision path and method-property bank visible. Let students annotate particle types and regions. Provide sentence frames that require claim, evidence, and reasoning.
extend: Ask students to propose an additional test that could challenge a classification, compare two viable separation sequences, or identify a limitation in a particle representation.

release_scope.standards_claim: Supports the NGSS practices of Developing and Using Models and Analyzing and Interpreting Data; no formal performance-expectation alignment is claimed.
release_scope.difference_from_existing_sku: This complete Chapter 2 unit includes explicit instruction, projectable slides, guided and independent practice, cumulative review, two 20-item tests, and rationale keys. It is distinct from Chapter 1 quantitative measurement work and from all legacy drafts; no scored prompt is reused.

lessons.title: Matter at Two Scales
lessons.target: Use the definition of matter and a particle model to make and limit claims about a sample.
lessons.engage: Air is invisible, light is visible, and sound can be heard. Which of the three is matter, and what evidence should decide?
lessons.big_idea: Matter has mass and occupies space. Particle models help explain composition and distribution, but their symbols, colors, spacing, and scale are simplified.

terms.definition: anything that has mass and occupies space
the scale of observations made directly or with ordinary tools
a simplified representation of particles and their arrangement
a feature of reality that a representation does not show accurately

teach_points: Use mass and occupied space—not visibility—as the classroom test for matter.
A particle symbol represents a type of particle; repeated symbols can reveal composition and distribution.
Identical particles support a pure-substance claim, while more than one particle type supports a mixture claim.
Models are not to scale and do not prove every property of the real sample.

visuals.caption: Particle types and distribution provide model evidence.

worked_example.prompt: A sealed diagram contains identical two-atom particles. What can be concluded, and what remains unknown?
steps: Every represented particle is identical, so the model supports a pure-substance claim.
Inspect the atom symbols inside one particle: the same element would indicate an element; different elements would indicate a compound.
If the symbols do not distinguish atom identity, the model lacks the evidence needed for the second decision.
worked_example.answer: The sample is modeled as pure. Element versus compound cannot be decided without evidence about the atom types in each particle.

lessons.cfu: Why does visibility not determine whether something is matter?

practice.prompt: Classify air in a sealed syringe, visible light, and sound as matter or not matter. Defend each decision.
practice.scaffold: Apply both parts of the definition: mass and occupied space.
practice.answer: Air is matter because it has mass and occupies space. Visible light and sound are forms of energy/waves, not samples of matter in this classroom classification.

practice.prompt: In the particle visual, what evidence distinguishes a homogeneous mixture from a heterogeneous mixture?
practice.answer: Both have more than one particle type. The homogeneous mixture is uniformly distributed; the heterogeneous mixture has nonuniform regions or clustering.

practice.prompt: State one useful feature and one limitation of the particle visual.
practice.answer: Useful: it makes composition and distribution visible. Limitation: particle sizes, colors, spacing, and two-dimensional positions are simplified and not to scale.

practice.prompt: A sample expands to fill its container. Explain why this observation alone does not prove it is not matter.
practice.answer: A gas can expand to fill a container and is still matter because it has mass and occupies space.

practice.prompt: What additional evidence is needed to decide whether identical two-atom particles represent an element or a compound?
practice.answer: Determine whether the two atoms in each particle are the same element or different elements.

lessons.misconception: Only solids and liquids are matter because gases cannot always be seen.
lessons.repair: Use a sealed syringe or inflated balloon as evidence that gas occupies space and contributes mass.

lessons.title: Classify Matter by Composition
lessons.target: Classify elements, compounds, homogeneous mixtures, and heterogeneous mixtures from composition evidence.
lessons.engage: A clear saltwater sample looks uniform. Does uniform appearance prove that it is a pure substance?
lessons.big_idea: Classification depends on how many substances are present, whether composition is fixed, and whether multiple components are uniformly distributed.

terms.definition: matter with constant composition and characteristic properties
a pure substance made of one chemical element
a pure substance containing elements chemically combined in fixed proportions
a physical combination of substances with variable composition

teach_points: First decide pure substance versus mixture; then choose the more specific label.
An element contains one element type; a compound contains different elements chemically combined in a fixed composition.
A homogeneous mixture is uniform at the sampled scale but still contains multiple substances.
A heterogeneous mixture has nonuniform composition or visibly distinct regions. Physical separation evidence supports a mixture claim.

visuals.caption: Visible mineral regions make granite nonuniform at this scale.

worked_example.prompt: A clear saltwater sample leaves salt after the water is removed by a physical process. Classify the original sample.
steps: The sample appears uniform, so it is homogeneous at the observed scale.
A physical process recovers components, which supports the presence of more than one substance.
Uniform distribution plus multiple substances identifies a homogeneous mixture.
worked_example.answer: Saltwater is a homogeneous mixture, not a pure compound.

lessons.cfu: Why are the words homogeneous and pure not interchangeable?

practice.prompt: Classify a clean copper wire as element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture. Explain.
practice.scaffold: Ask whether the sample contains one element type or more than one substance.
practice.answer: Element. A clean copper sample consists of one chemical element, Cu.

practice.prompt: Classify distilled water and explain why it is not an element.
practice.answer: Compound. Pure water has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed composition as H2O.

practice.prompt: Classify clean, well-mixed air at one location. Explain why uniform does not mean pure.
practice.answer: Homogeneous mixture. It is uniform at the sampled scale but contains multiple substances, including nitrogen, oxygen, argon, and others.

practice.prompt: Classify granite with visibly different mineral regions.
practice.answer: Heterogeneous mixture because composition is not uniform across the visible sample.

practice.prompt: A model has two particle types evenly intermingled. Give the most specific label and two pieces of evidence.
practice.answer: Homogeneous mixture: more than one particle type is present, and the types are uniformly distributed.

lessons.misconception: A sample that looks uniform must be a pure substance.
lessons.repair: Ask whether a physical separation or particle model reveals more than one component before using the word pure.

lessons.title: Properties Describe Matter
lessons.target: Classify physical and chemical properties and distinguish intensive from extensive properties.
lessons.engage: Copper conducts electricity and can react with oxygen. Which statement can be checked without changing copper into a new substance?
lessons.big_idea: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing chemical identity; a chemical property describes the ability to undergo a chemical change.

terms.definition: a characteristic observed or measured without changing identity
the ability of a substance to undergo a chemical change
a property independent of sample amount under stated conditions
a property that depends on the amount of sample

teach_points: Color, density, melting point, and conductivity are physical properties when measured without changing identity.
Flammability and reactivity describe possible chemical behavior, even when no reaction is occurring at that moment.
Mass and volume are extensive because they change with sample amount.
Density and melting point are intensive under the same stated conditions and can help identify a substance.

visuals.caption: Color and luster are observable physical properties of copper.
Flammability describes the ability to burn; the property exists before ignition.

worked_example.prompt: Classify density and mass as physical or chemical and as intensive or extensive.
steps: Both can be measured without changing chemical identity, so both are physical properties.
Density remains characteristic when sample amount changes under the same conditions, so it is intensive.
Mass increases or decreases with sample amount, so it is extensive.
worked_example.answer: Density is physical and intensive; mass is physical and extensive.

lessons.cfu: Why can flammability be stated as a property before a flame is present?

practice.prompt: Classify melting point as physical or chemical and intensive or extensive.
practice.scaffold: Ask whether identity changes during measurement and whether the value depends on sample amount.
practice.answer: Physical and intensive under the same pressure and purity conditions.

practice.prompt: Classify volume as physical or chemical and intensive or extensive.
practice.answer: Physical and extensive because measuring volume does not require a new substance and volume depends on amount.

practice.prompt: Classify flammability and explain why it is not a physical property.
practice.answer: Chemical property. It describes the ability to react by burning and form new substances.

practice.prompt: A lab card says 'Copper conducts electric current.' Is this a property or a change? Classify it.
practice.answer: It is a physical property; conductivity can be observed without changing copper into a new substance.

practice.prompt: Why is density often more useful for identification than volume?
practice.answer: Density is intensive and can remain characteristic under stated conditions, while volume changes with sample amount.

lessons.misconception: The word chemical in a material's name makes every listed characteristic a chemical property.
lessons.repair: Use the identity-change test: could the characteristic be measured while the substance remains the same substance?

lessons.title: Physical or Chemical Change?
lessons.target: Classify changes by the new-substance criterion and evaluate common clues in context.
lessons.engage: Bubbles appear when a cold soda is opened and when two reacting solutions are mixed. Do bubbles prove the same kind of change in both cases?
lessons.big_idea: A chemical change forms one or more new substances. Color, gas, precipitate, light, odor, or temperature change can support a claim but is not automatic proof.

terms.definition: a change in form or state that does not require a new substance
a process in which atoms rearrange to form new substances
an observation or result used to support or challenge a claim
matter is not created or destroyed in a closed-system chemical change

teach_points: Melting, freezing, crushing, dissolving in a recoverable context, and physical separation do not by themselves require a new substance.
Burning, decomposition, and reactions that form products with new compositions are chemical changes.
A clue must be compared with alternatives: bubbles may be a gas product, boiling, or released dissolved gas.
An open container may lose gaseous products from measurement; this does not violate conservation of matter.

visuals.caption: Melting changes state while the substance remains water.
Burning forms new substances and is chemical.

worked_example.prompt: Salt dissolves in water and is later recovered by evaporating the water. Classify the process in this context.
steps: Dissolving produces a uniform solution but does not by itself establish a new substance.
The original salt is recovered by a physical method.
Recovery supports a physical-change/separation claim for this classroom context.
worked_example.answer: Physical change and physical separation in this context.

lessons.cfu: Name one nonchemical process that can produce bubbles.

practice.prompt: Ice melts in a sealed bag. Classify the change and identify what remains the same.
practice.scaffold: Ask whether the substance's chemical identity changes.
practice.answer: Physical change. The substance remains H2O; only its physical state changes.

practice.prompt: Candle wax burns in oxygen and produces different substances. Classify the change and cite decisive evidence.
practice.answer: Chemical change because atoms are rearranged into new substances such as carbon dioxide and water vapor.

practice.prompt: A tablet is crushed into powder without reacting. Classify the change.
practice.answer: Physical change; size and surface area change, but no new substance is required.

practice.prompt: Explain why bubbles support but do not by themselves prove a chemical-change claim.
practice.answer: Bubbles may be a gas product, but boiling or release of dissolved gas can also make bubbles; context and additional evidence are needed.

practice.prompt: A solid is strongly heated in an open container and a gas escapes. Why can the measured solid mass decrease without violating conservation?
practice.answer: Some product matter leaves as gas. Total matter is conserved when all products are included, but the open container does not retain every product.

lessons.misconception: Any color change, temperature change, or bubble formation automatically proves a chemical reaction.
lessons.repair: Require students to name the proposed new substance or rule out a physical alternative before accepting the claim.

lessons.title: Separate Mixtures by Properties
lessons.target: Choose and sequence physical separation methods from differences in particle size, solubility, volatility, magnetism, or phase behavior.
lessons.engage: A beaker contains iron filings, salt, sand, and water. Which separation should happen first, and why does order matter?
lessons.big_idea: A separation method works because components differ in a physical property. A good plan names both the method and the property difference.

terms.definition: separation using particle size and insolubility
separation using differences in volatility or boiling behavior
separation using different attractions and travel rates
separation by carefully pouring one phase from another

teach_points: Use magnetism before adding water when a dry magnetic component is present.
Use filtration for an insoluble solid in a liquid; dissolved solute passes with the liquid.
Use distillation when the goal includes collecting the more volatile liquid as well as the residue.
Use chromatography to test whether a soluble colored sample contains components with different attractions and travel rates.

visuals.caption: Residue remains on the filter; filtrate passes through.
Vapor is condensed and collected during simple distillation.
Immiscible liquid layers can be drained separately.

worked_example.prompt: A uniform blue liquid yields colorless liquid and blue solid after distillation. What claim is supported?
steps: The original sample appears homogeneous, but appearance alone cannot establish purity.
Distillation is a physical method based on volatility or boiling behavior.
Recovering two components by a physical process supports a mixture claim.
worked_example.answer: The original sample is a homogeneous mixture with at least two components.

lessons.cfu: Why does filtration fail to remove salt dissolved in water?

practice.prompt: Choose a method to separate insoluble sand from water and name the property difference.
practice.scaffold: Decide whether the solid is dissolved and whether its particles can be retained.
practice.answer: Filtration; sand is insoluble and its particles are retained while water passes through.

practice.prompt: A saltwater sample must yield both water and salt. Choose a method and explain why evaporation alone is incomplete.
practice.answer: Distillation. It collects condensed water and leaves salt; evaporation alone may recover salt but does not collect the water.

practice.prompt: Choose a method to test whether black marker ink contains more than one dye.
practice.answer: Paper chromatography; components travel differently because of different attractions to the mobile and stationary phases.

practice.prompt: Choose the first method for a dry mixture of iron filings and table salt.
practice.answer: Magnetic separation; a magnet attracts iron but not salt.

practice.prompt: Explain why separating a mixture is usually physical even when several steps are required.
practice.answer: The methods exploit physical-property differences and recover components without requiring their chemical identities to change.

lessons.misconception: One separation method should remove every component from any mixture.
lessons.repair: Build a method-property table and choose one step for one property difference at a time; then reevaluate the remaining mixture.

review.prompt: Explain why air is matter even though it is usually invisible.
review.answer: Air has mass and occupies space; visibility is not part of the definition of matter.

review.prompt: A particle model shows one repeated particle made of two different atom types. Classify the sample.
review.answer: A pure compound: one particle type is present, and each particle contains different elements chemically combined.

review.prompt: Classify salad dressing with visible oil and water layers.
review.answer: Heterogeneous mixture because composition is nonuniform and distinct phases are visible.

review.prompt: Classify electrical conductivity and flammability as physical or chemical properties.
review.answer: Conductivity is physical; flammability is chemical.

review.prompt: Explain why mass is extensive but density is intensive.
review.answer: Mass depends on sample amount; density can remain characteristic as amount changes under the same conditions.

review.prompt: Classify boiling water and burning paper as physical or chemical changes.
review.answer: Boiling water is physical; burning paper is chemical because new substances form.

review.prompt: Bubbles form when a liquid is warmed. What additional evidence is needed before claiming a chemical change?
review.answer: Rule out boiling or released dissolved gas and seek evidence of a new substance, such as a product with a new composition or properties.

review.prompt: Choose a method for oil and water layers and name the property evidence.
review.answer: Decantation or a separatory funnel; immiscibility creates separate phases, and density helps determine their layering.

review.prompt: A distillation starts with 120.0 g and recovers 92.0 g liquid plus 27.6 g solid. Calculate percent recovery.
Why can a uniform appearance support but not prove a homogeneous-mixture classification?
review.answer: Appearance shows uniformity only at the observed scale; purity and dissolved components require additional evidence.

A.stem: Which sample is matter?
A.rationale: Air has mass and occupies space, so it is matter.

A.stem: A particle model contains two particle types evenly distributed. What is the best classification?
A.rationale: More than one particle type indicates a mixture, and uniform distribution makes it homogeneous.

A.stem: Which statement describes a limitation of a typical particle model?
choices: Particle size and spacing are not shown to scale.
It can never show more than one particle type.
It proves every property of the sample.
A.rationale: Classroom particle diagrams simplify size, spacing, color, and dimensionality.

A.stem: Which evidence best supports that a clear solution is a mixture?
choices: A physical process recovers two components.
A.rationale: Physical recovery of components supports the presence of more than one substance.

A.stem: How should a clean copper wire be classified?
A.rationale: Clean copper consists of one chemical element, Cu.

A.stem: How should pure water be classified?
A.rationale: Water contains hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed composition.

A.stem: Why is well-mixed air not a pure substance?
A.rationale: Air can be uniform while containing nitrogen, oxygen, argon, and other substances.

A.stem: Granite with visibly different mineral regions is a
A.rationale: Distinct mineral regions show nonuniform composition.

A.stem: Which property is physical and intensive?
A.rationale: Density can be measured without changing identity and does not depend on sample amount under the same conditions.

A.stem: Which property is chemical?
A.rationale: Flammability describes the ability to react by burning and form new substances.

A.stem: Which property depends on sample amount?
A.rationale: Mass is extensive and changes with the amount of sample.

A.stem: Which process is a physical change?
A.rationale: Melting changes physical state while the substance remains H2O.

A.stem: Which observation is decisive evidence of a chemical change?
choices: New substances with different compositions form.
A.rationale: Formation of new substances is the defining criterion for a chemical change.

A.stem: Why do bubbles not always prove a chemical reaction?
A.rationale: A phase change or release of dissolved gas can produce bubbles without a chemical reaction.

A.stem: Which method separates insoluble sand from water?
A.rationale: Filtration retains insoluble particles while the liquid passes through.

A.stem: Which method should be used to collect both water and salt from saltwater?
A.rationale: Distillation collects condensed water while salt remains.

A.stem: Which method tests whether marker ink contains multiple dyes?
A.rationale: Chromatography separates soluble components by different attractions and travel rates.

A.stem: What is the best first step for dry iron filings mixed with salt?
A.rationale: Magnetism selectively removes iron before additional steps are needed.

A.stem: A 120.0 g sample yields 92.0 g liquid and 27.6 g solid. What is percent recovery?
Why may solid mass decrease when heating occurs in an open container?
choices: A gaseous product may leave the container.
A.rationale: An open system may not retain gaseous products; total matter is conserved when all products are included.

B.stem: Which observation is not evidence that something is matter?
B.rationale: Visibility is not part of the definition; invisible gases can be matter.

B.stem: A model contains only identical particles made of two different atom types. What is the best classification?
B.rationale: One repeated particle type supports purity; different elements bonded in each particle support a compound.

B.stem: What does a particle model most directly help students inspect?
B.rationale: Symbols and arrangement provide model evidence about particle types and distribution.

B.stem: A clear liquid leaves two recoverable substances after a physical separation. It is best classified as a
B.rationale: The clear sample is uniform, while physical recovery of components shows it is a mixture.

B.stem: Which sample is a compound?
B.rationale: Pure water contains hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

B.stem: Which sample is a homogeneous mixture?
B.rationale: Well-mixed air contains multiple substances distributed uniformly at the sampled scale.

B.stem: Which sample is heterogeneous?
B.rationale: Visible immiscible layers show nonuniform composition.

B.stem: Which result would most strongly challenge a claim that a sample is pure?
choices: A physical method separates two components.
B.rationale: Recovering components physically supports a mixture rather than a pure substance.

B.stem: Which pair contains two physical properties?
B.rationale: Density and conductivity can be measured without changing chemical identity.

B.stem: Which property is extensive?
B.rationale: Volume depends on the amount of sample present.

B.stem: Why is flammability a property even before ignition?
B.rationale: A property can describe a substance's ability to undergo a change without the change occurring during the statement.

B.stem: Which process is a chemical change?
choices: Wax burns and forms new substances.
B.rationale: Burning rearranges atoms and forms products with new compositions.

B.stem: Which observation alone is insufficient to prove a chemical change?
B.rationale: Bubbles can also result from boiling or release of dissolved gas.

B.stem: Why is crushing a solid usually a physical change?
choices: Its size changes without requiring a new substance.
B.rationale: Crushing changes size and surface area, not chemical identity.

B.stem: Which method separates two immiscible liquid layers?
B.rationale: Separate phases can be drained or poured apart; density helps determine layering.

B.stem: Why does filtration not remove dissolved salt from water?
choices: Dissolved particles pass with the liquid.
B.rationale: A filter retains insoluble particles but does not ordinarily remove dissolved solute.

B.stem: Which property difference is central to distillation?
B.rationale: Components vaporize and condense differently because their volatility or boiling behavior differs.

B.stem: Which sequence is best for dry iron filings mixed with sand?
choices: Use a magnet, then evaluate the sand.
B.rationale: Magnetism selectively removes iron from a dry nonmagnetic solid.

B.stem: A uniform blue liquid leaves no filter residue but yields liquid and solid by distillation. What is the best claim?
choices: It is a homogeneous mixture with dissolved material.
B.rationale: No residue is expected for dissolved solute, while distillation physically recovers components.

B.stem: Which statement correctly applies conservation of matter?
choices: Gas products count even if they leave an open container.
Conservation applies only to physical changes.
B.rationale: All products, including gases, must be included when accounting for matter.
